title: Depth-First Search
summary: Follow one graph path before returning to try another. Trace depth-first search safely around a cycle in six complete language examples.
introduction: Imagine exploring a maze with a pencil. Follow one passage as far as you can. When there is no new room to enter, return to the last choice and try another passage. Depth-first search, or DFS, uses this deep-first plan.
learningObjectives: Trace recursive visits and returns through a graph
Use seen marks to stop repeated visits around cycles

blocks.text: DFS explores one unvisited neighbour immediately before trying the next neighbour. Recursion lets the function call itself for that next node. Waiting calls remember where to return when a path ends.

A seen mark records that a node has been visited. Mark before exploring neighbours so a link back to an earlier node is skipped. This makes the algorithm safe on cycles, routes that return to a previous node.
The graph has the same links as the BFS lesson: 0-1, 0-2, 1-3, and 2-3, all in both directions. Neighbours are stored in the same order in every language.

items: Visit and mark 0. Its first neighbour is 1, so visit 1 next.
At 1, skip the already seen 0. Follow the other neighbour, 3.
At 3, skip seen node 1 and follow node 2. At 2, both neighbours 0 and 3 are seen, so return.
Return from 3 and then 1 to 0. Node 0's remaining neighbour, 2, is already seen. Stop with order 0, 1, 3, 2.

blocks.text: The same program in six languages

Choose the language you are learning. Each tab solves the same problem and prints the same result. JavaScript can run in this page. The other tabs need separate local tools: a C11 compiler, a C++17 compiler, Python 3, .NET 8 or later for C#, or Java 17. Use Program.cs for C# and Main.java for Java.

variants.code:
graph = [[1, 2], [0, 3], [0, 3], [1, 2]]
seen = [False] * len(graph)
order = []

def visit(current):
    seen[current] = True
    order.append(current)
    for next_node in graph[current]:
        if not seen[next_node]:
            visit(next_node)

visit(0)
print(*order)

blocks.text: DFS reaches 3 through 1 before visiting 2, even though 2 is next to the start. Returning from a call does not print the node again; each node is recorded only on its first visit.

Node 0 must exist, and each neighbour number must refer to a real node. In C, each row holds exactly two neighbours for this particular graph, and the output array holds four nodes. A general graph needs separate neighbour counts and enough storage.

A disconnected graph may contain nodes unreachable from 0. To cover them all, start another visit from every still-unseen node without clearing the marks. The exact visit order depends on the neighbour order.

DFS does not generally find a shortest route. A long graph path can also make too many recursive calls. An explicit stack, where you store pending nodes yourself, can avoid a language's recursion limit.
How much work and extra room?

Let V count nodes and E count links. With adjacency lists, each reachable node is entered once, and each of its neighbour entries is checked once. With setup included, a whole connected graph takes O(V + E) time.
The seen marks, saved output, and deepest chain of waiting calls each use at most O(V) space. The total extra space is O(V). A cycle adds no extra visits because seen blocks repeated entries.

blocks.title: Try one small change
blocks.text: Swap node 0's neighbours from [1, 2] to [2, 1]. Keep other rows the same. Trace 0 to 2 to 3 to 1, then check for output 0 2 3 1.

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.text: Do not wait until after visiting neighbours to mark the current node. On a cycle, a neighbour can call back into a still-unmarked node, creating repeated calls. Mark first, then explore.
